items.title: Tom Malone interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2023
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...we all had aspirations to maybe get in a big band, oh my God if we could get in Buddy Rich’s big band.

ctx.x: in walking distance. So if we showed up ten minutes late we all showed up together and we got the job done. So even though that happened occasionally — I got into the business in New York — I met Bill Watrous early on and he would send me in to sub for him, to cover. I’d show up and I’d say, “Bill Watrous will be here in ten minutes,” and I’d play until he got there. And that’s the way I established myself in the business. Yeah. Bill Watrous and I became friends. I was playing trombone with a group called…

You just said something that I wanted to follow up on. The group of people that I graduated with, we all had aspirations to maybe get in a big band, oh my God if we could get in Buddy Rich’s big band. Most of them took the fall-back position and became public school teachers, which is an honorable, you know, position. But for those of you in that group that had aspirations to be jazz musicians, to have a band, to record for Blue Note, like your musical heroes did, but now you’re playing two, three, four sessions…

Well you make plans in your life based on what’s going on around you at the time. But everything changes and you have to be willing to change with the style of music. I know when I first got to New York, 1970, the studio recording scene was in a transition from big band and jazz to rock & roll. And there were a lot of guys like bass players, drummers — oh this rock & roll thing’s never going to catch on, I don’t want to play that junk. You know they used a different word. And so, and those guys were out of the…
